description: Hi everyone, I‘m a founder with years of AI experience (and I love space) looking for technical teammates to start this journey together :) I am competitive yes but I’m not gonna lose my mind over winning this xd I want to give the challenge a good shot while connecting with many capable teammates. I am also looking for cofounders for my startup so it would be cool to meet capable people
summary:
ODIN is a map for an astronaut's first walk on Mars. It turns NASA orbit images, terrain and rover measurements into one tool with three places. At the Station you turn a globe of Mars, choose a region and a task, and look at planet-wide data such as geology, temperature, thorium and potassium. On the Tablet you set a destination and the app plans a route on a 1 m terrain grid. The route keeps to a slope limit and the suit time and goes around no-go areas. If no safe route exists, the app says why and offers a fix. In the Helmet you follow the route with a compass, a round minimap and marked hazard areas, and a dust or solar particle scenario draws the way back to the habitat.

The challenge asks for a map that helps people survive on Mars. Our answer is a map that needs no training: a two minute tour on the real controls teaches the whole app. It matters because the data already exists in separate archives, and an astronaut on foot has no time to search them. The app runs fully in the browser, with no account and no server.
details:
What it does:

ODIN is a web app with three places that follow an astronaut's day.

Station: a globe of Mars with three regions (Gale Boxwork, Gale Bradbury, Jezero). You choose a region and a task. The task switches on the data it needs and leaves the rest off. Planet-wide layers show geology, temperature, thorium, potassium and hydrogen, and you can import your own data set.

Tablet: a local map on a 25 cm orbit image. You set a destination and the route plans itself on the terrain grid. You see distance, time and the steepest slope, and you can compare the shortest and the easiest route. You can also load the path the Curiosity rover really drove and compare it with the planned route. A prepared science walk at the boxwork ridges has 8 stops, 1.7 km and 4 h 00 min in the suit.

Helmet: a first-person view of the terrain with a compass, a round minimap, hatched hazard areas and the next stop. Warnings are short and wait in a list. You can simulate a dust event or a solar particle event; the app then draws the way back to the habitat. Before you go outside, you can watch the whole route in 90 seconds.

How it works:

All terrain, images and measurements are prepared files that load in the browser. The route planner is our own code. It runs in a Web Worker on the height and slope grid and respects a slope limit, a time limit and no-go areas. There is no server and no account. Every value in the app shows its source, unit and time when you ask for it.

Benefits and intended impact:

An astronaut on foot has a suit clock, a slope limit and no rescue team. The data that keeps them safe exists, but in separate archives and formats. ODIN puts it on one map that takes two minutes to learn. The same app lets students and the public plan a walk on real Mars terrain, which makes the data of the missions easy to explore.

Astronaut safety comes first in ODIN. A route is only offered if it keeps to the slope limit, the suit time and the no-go areas; if none exists, the app says why and offers the safe change. The helmet shows hazard areas and short warnings, and it draws the way back to the habitat when a dust or solar particle event starts. The limits come from NASA sources, and every simulated value is labelled as simulated.

How it is creative:

One app covers the whole chain from the planet view to a single step on the ground. Each task preset turns on only the data that task needs. Every blocked action says why and offers the fix. The check against Curiosity's real path shows that the planned routes are credible. A guided tour runs on the real controls, not in a video.

What we considered:

- Accessibility: no installation, no account, any modern browser, works on a laptop or a tablet, keyboard control, short plain texts.
- Cost and energy: the app is a static website. It needs no backend and no paid service, and all planning runs on the user's device.
- Honesty of the data: measured values are separate from simulated ones. Hazard events are labelled "scenario". The weather outlook is labelled "simulated". Limits that come from a NASA standard or a paper name that source.
- Limits: the routes are a planning aid, not a flight-qualified safety system. The terrain data does not show every small obstacle.

Tools and languages:

TypeScript, React, Vite, CesiumJS (globe), three.js (first-person terrain), Python (data preparation). Code hosting and the live site: GitHub and GitHub Pages.

Use of AI:

We built the app with AI coding assistants (Claude by Anthropic and OpenAI Codex). They wrote code, tests and documentation from our design decisions, and we reviewed and tested the results. The slide text was drafted with AI and edited by the team. All Mars imagery, terrain and measurements are real data from NASA, USGS and ESA. The app contains no AI-generated images.
